opts.title: Fitting a quotation to your sentence

segments.why: Brackets show the reader you changed will to would to fit a past-tense sentence.

segments: little note, nor long remember” what was said that day.

blocks.cap: A change to a quoted word goes in brackets. (Gettysburg Address: “The world will little note, nor long remember what we say here.”)

blocks.html: Fit the quotation to your sentence, but never change its meaning. Changed or added words go in brackets; cut words are marked with an ellipsis; what is left must say what the source said.

Quotation marks are a promise: these are the source’s exact words. Brackets and ellipses keep the promise while letting you fit the words to your sentence. Without them, a reader who checks the source will find words that don’t match, and stop trusting you.

blocks.title: Cut fairly
blocks.q: Douglass: “For it is not light that is needed, but fire.” A student writes: Douglass says “it is … light that is needed.” What went wrong?
steps: The ellipsis cut “not,” so the quotation now says the opposite of what Douglass said.
An ellipsis may remove words only when the meaning stays the same.
A fair version: Douglass says that “it is not light that is needed, but fire.”
blocks.a: The cut reversed the meaning; that misrepresents the source.

blocks.title: Add a clarifying word
blocks.q: Quote “To him, your celebration is a sham” so readers know who “him” is.
steps: Out of context, “him” is unclear.
Add the clarification in brackets right after it: “To him [the enslaved person], your celebration is a sham.”
Brackets tell the reader those words are yours.
blocks.a: Douglass argues that “[t]o him [the enslaved person], your celebration is a sham.”

blocks.html: Changing a quotation’s words without brackets, or cutting words without an ellipsis. Both make the quotation look like the source’s exact words when it isn’t. Styles differ on small details, such as spacing in an ellipsis and whether to bracket a changed first capital, so follow the style your teacher assigns; but every style marks changes. Check each quotation against the source, word for word.

blocks.html: The synthesis essay joins the argument essay and integrated sources. You read a set of sources on an issue, take your own position, and support it with several of them, citing each. On the AP English Language exam, the synthesis question gives a set of sources and asks students to use at least three.

blocks.name: wr-essay
blocks.cap: A synthesis essay is organized by your reasons, with sources serving each one.

blocks.html: Your argument organizes the essay; the sources serve it. Each body paragraph makes one of your claims and brings in the sources that support or challenge it, in conversation with each other.

If the sources organize the essay, you have written a series of summaries, and your own position gets lost. If your reasons organize it, each source becomes evidence for something you are arguing, and the reader sees your thinking at every step.

Organized by reasons

¶3 After-school costs need a plan (C and D agree; propose shifting practices).

blocks.title: A synthesis sentence
blocks.q: Using the practice sources from the last topic, write one sentence that puts two sources in conversation to support the claim that a later start is worth its costs.
steps: Choose two sources that relate: A (sleep benefit) and B (bus cost) answer different questions.
Name both and say how they relate: A shows the benefit; B shows the cost.
Add your own judgment: which matters more, and why.
blocks.a: “While the district’s memo (Source B) shows that a later start would require more buses, the sleep research (Source A) suggests the benefit reaches every student every morning, a gain that outweighs a cost the district can plan for.”

blocks.html: Letting the sources organize the essay, one paragraph per source. Check your topic sentences: if any of them begins with a source (“Source C says …”), rewrite it to state your claim, then bring in the sources as support.
In the AP exam’s synthesis question, sources are cited by letter, such as (Source A), or by author; in a research paper, use the style your teacher assigns, as in Composition’s MLA in-text citations.

blocks.html: In Composition you learned to cut wordiness. Diction goes further: choosing each word for what it means exactly, what it suggests, and how formal it sounds, always for the audience and purpose at hand.

head: Praise
Neutral
Criticism

careful with money

blocks.html: Good diction is precise (the exact word, not a vague one), fitting in connotation (the feeling the word carries), and fitting in formality (the level of language the audience expects).

Readers react to connotation before they think about meaning. Call a neighbor “thrifty” and you praise her; call her “stingy” and you have picked a fight, though both words say she spends little. Precise words also save readers work: “the bus was 25 minutes late” tells them more than “the bus was really late.”

blocks.title: Lincoln’s three verbs
blocks.q: Gettysburg: “we can not dedicate—we can not consecrate—we can not hallow—this ground.” Why three verbs that mean nearly the same thing?
steps: Dedicate means to set apart for a purpose: an ordinary civic word.
Consecrate means to make sacred: a religious word.
Hallow is older and holier still, the word of the Lord’s Prayer (“hallowed be thy name”).
The diction climbs from civic to sacred, so the soldiers’ deeds seem holier with each step.
blocks.a: The verbs rise in connotation, from civic to sacred, so the ground grows holier as the sentence goes.

blocks.title: Make it precise
blocks.q: Revise: “The new park is really nice and has a lot of good stuff.”
steps: Really nice and good stuff are vague: what, exactly?
Name the things: a splash pad, shaded benches, a quarter-mile walking loop.
Choose a precise judgment: welcoming, shady, busy?
blocks.a: “The new park is welcoming: a splash pad, shaded benches and a quarter-mile walking loop.”

blocks.html: Choosing a thesaurus word whose connotation doesn’t fit. Thrifty and stingy both mean careful with money, but only one is praise. Notorious means famous for something bad, so “our notorious science fair” insults the fair. Check each new word in a dictionary’s example sentences before you use it.

blocks.html: After choosing the right words (diction), cut the words that do no work. You started this in Composition’s Concise Writing. In 1918 William Strunk Jr. put the rule in three words: “Omit needless words.”

His explanation is worth reading whole: “Vigorous writing is concise. A sentence should contain no unnecessary words, a paragraph no unnecessary sentences, for the same reason that a drawing should have no unnecessary lines and a machine no unnecessary parts. This requires not that the writer make all his sentences short, or that he avoid all detail and treat his subjects only in outline, but that every word tell.”

head: Wordy (Strunk’s examples, 1918)
Concise

whether

blocks.cap: From Rule 13 of The Elements of Style (1918).

items: Redundancy: saying it twice (past history, end result, each and every, completely finished).
Empty phrases: owing to the fact that, at this point in time, in order to.
Weak openings: There is …, It is … that, which delay the real subject and verb.
Throat-clearing: In my opinion, I think that, It is important to note that.

blocks.html: Make every word tell. Cut redundancy, empty phrases, weak openings and throat-clearing, but keep the details that carry meaning.

Every needless word spends a little of the reader’s attention and gives nothing back. Concise prose also sounds more confident: “Because it rained, we stayed in” is surer than “Owing to the fact that it was raining, we made the decision to remain inside.”

opts.after: Many students say the late bus is too crowded.

blocks.title: Cut, but keep the meaning
blocks.q: Revise: “In my opinion, I think that the end result of the new schedule is that each and every student has more time to eat lunch.”
steps: “In my opinion, I think that” is throat-clearing; the reader knows it is your opinion.
“End result” and “each and every” are redundant.
“The end result of … is that” is an empty frame around the real claim.
blocks.a: “The new schedule gives every student more time for lunch.”

blocks.html: Thinking longer sounds smarter, and padding sentences with phrases that add no meaning. Readers notice padding, and it buries your point. But concision isn’t the same as shortness: Strunk said the rule does not mean avoiding detail. Check: for each phrase, ask “What would the reader lose without it?” If nothing, cut it.

blocks.html: In Usage you learned to tell active from passive voice. This topic is about choosing between them. Strunk’s Rule 11 is “Use the active voice,” and his reason holds up: “The active voice is usually more direct and vigorous than the passive.” Like concision, it is about getting the doer and the action to the reader quickly.

head: Active
Passive
rows: The committee approved the budget.
The budget was approved by the committee.
Someone stole my bike.
My bike was stolen.
Volunteers planted forty trees.
Forty trees were planted (by volunteers).
blocks.cap: In the passive, the receiver of the action becomes the subject, and the doer moves to a by-phrase or disappears.

blocks.html: But Strunk himself added: “This rule does not, of course, mean that the writer should entirely discard the passive voice, which is frequently convenient and sometimes necessary.” His example: “The dramatists of the Restoration are little esteemed to-day” fits a paragraph about the dramatists; “Modern readers have little esteem for the dramatists of the Restoration” fits a paragraph about modern readers.
Prefer the active voice when the doer matters. Use the passive when the doer is unknown or unimportant, or to keep the paragraph’s focus on what was acted on.

A sentence’s subject is what it is about. The voice lets you choose which noun is the subject, so the right voice is whichever puts the paragraph’s topic first. That is a reason, not a rule of taste, and it explains both Strunk’s rule and his exception.

blocks.title: When the passive is right
blocks.q: Which is better in a paragraph about the old stone bridge: (A) “Local stonemasons built the bridge in 1911.” (B) “The bridge was built in 1911 by local stonemasons.”
steps: The paragraph is about the bridge, so the bridge should be the subject.
B keeps the focus on the bridge and still names the builders.
In a paragraph about the stonemasons’ work, A would be better.
blocks.a: B, because the paragraph is about the bridge.

blocks.title: When the passive hides something
blocks.q: A company note says: “Mistakes were made in the billing.” What is missing?
steps: The passive with no by-phrase leaves out who made the mistakes.
Sometimes that is fine (the doer is unknown). Here, readers want to know who is responsible.
Active version: “Our billing team made mistakes, and we are fixing them.”
blocks.a: The doer; the active version takes responsibility.

blocks.html: Two opposite slips. Some writers hear “never use the passive” and force awkward active sentences (“Someone unknown to us stole the bike”). Others use the passive to hide who did something. Check: who did it, does the reader need to know, and what is this paragraph about? Let those answers choose the voice.

blocks.html: In Grammar you built compound-complex sentences; in Concision you cut needless words. Sentence variety puts the shapes to work: a mix of lengths and structures that keeps readers alert and shows how your ideas connect.

blocks.name: wr-revise

opts.before: The storm hit at noon. The power went out. The school closed early. The buses came at one. Everyone got home safely.
opts.after: When the storm hit at noon, the power went out, and the school closed early. The buses came at one. Everyone got home safely.

blocks.cap: Five choppy sentences become one longer sentence that shows how the events connect, then two short ones that land.

blocks.html: Vary sentence length and structure on purpose: longer sentences to connect related ideas, short ones for emphasis, and different openings so not every sentence starts with its subject.

A string of same-length sentences sounds like a drumbeat, and readers stop hearing it. Variety does more than add music: joining ideas shows their logic (cause, contrast, time), and a short sentence after long ones tells the reader “this matters.”

items: With the subject: The volunteers stacked sandbags all night.
With a phrase: Through the night, volunteers stacked sandbags.
With a dependent clause: As the creek rose, volunteers stacked sandbags.
With a participle phrase: Working through the night, volunteers stacked sandbags.

blocks.title: A short sentence for emphasis
blocks.q: Lincoln, 1865: “Both parties deprecated war; but one of them would make war rather than let the nation survive; and the other would accept war rather than let it perish. And the war came.” Why end with four words?
steps: The first sentence is long and balanced, weighing the two sides.
Then four plain words: “And the war came.”
The sudden short sentence lands like a blow, and makes the war seem to arrive on its own, after all the weighing.
blocks.a: The short sentence, after a long one, gives the war’s arrival the weight of a single blow.

blocks.html: Starting every sentence with the subject, or writing every sentence the same length, so the prose plods. The opposite slip is variety for its own sake: a fancy opening that hides the point. Check: read a paragraph aloud. Where it drones, combine; where an idea matters most, give it a short sentence.

blocks.html: Within a sentence, position is emphasis. Sentence variety works across sentences; this topic works inside one. Strunk’s Rule 18: “Place the emphatic words of a sentence at the end.” He explains: “The proper place for the word, or group of words, which the writer desires to make most prominent is usually the end of the sentence.”

head: Weaker (Strunk’s first version)
Stronger (his revision)
rows: Humanity has hardly advanced in fortitude since that time, though it has advanced in many other ways.
Humanity, since that time, has advanced in many other ways, but it has hardly advanced in fortitude.
This steel is principally used for making razors, because of its hardness.
Because of its hardness, this steel is principally used in making razors.
blocks.cap: Strunk’s examples (1918): the revision ends on the point.

blocks.html: Put the words you most want remembered at the end of the sentence. The beginning is the other strong position; the middle is the quietest.

Readers hold a sentence open until it ends, and the last words ring longest. Speakers know this too: the Gettysburg Address ends not on “the people” but on “shall not perish from the earth,” a solemn, final image.

The beginning of a sentence is the other strong position. Strunk notes that any element other than the subject “becomes emphatic when placed first,” as in his example “Deceit or treachery he could never forgive.” Use that inverted order rarely; it works because it is unusual.

opts.before: Students lose an hour of sleep every school day because of the early start, which is something to think about in today’s society.
opts.after: Because of the early start, students lose an hour of sleep every school day.

blocks.title: Move the point to the end
blocks.q: Revise so the danger is emphasized: “Children cross six lanes of traffic at Elm and Fifth with no light, according to the town’s report.”
steps: The sentence ends on its source, the least important part.
Move the source to the front.
End on the danger itself.
blocks.a: “According to the town’s report, children at Elm and Fifth cross six lanes of traffic with no light.”

blocks.html: Burying the key word in the middle, or ending on a weak phrase like “in today’s society,” “in my opinion,” or “and things like that.” Check the last three words of each important sentence: are they the words you want remembered? If not, rearrange.

blocks.html: Emphasis puts the new, important words at the end of a sentence. Cohesion is the other half: begin each sentence with something the reader already knows, often what the last sentence ended on. Linguists call this the order of given (old) and new information.

blocks.name: wr-revise

segments: Our town’s creek floods every April.

segments.del: Clogged storm drains upstream are the cause of the flooding.
segments.ins: The flooding comes from storm drains clogged upstream.
segments.why: Start with the flooding, which the reader just met; end with the new information, the clogged drains.

segments.del: Leaves from the park’s maples fill those drains each fall.
segments.ins: Those drains fill each fall with leaves from the park’s maples.
segments.why: Start with the drains (old), end with the leaves (new).

blocks.cap: Each revised sentence begins where the last one ended.

blocks.html: Begin a sentence with old information the reader already has, and end it with new information. Then the next sentence can begin with that new information, and the paragraph flows like a chain.

A reader needs a handhold to grab before taking in something new. When a sentence starts with something unfamiliar, the reader has to hold it in mind without knowing why it matters, and the prose feels choppy even when every sentence is correct.

blocks.title: Choose the next sentence
blocks.q: First sentence: “The library is adding Sunday hours this fall.” Which next sentence flows better? (A) “A four-weekend trial last spring drew 900 visitors, which led to the new hours.” (B) “The new hours grew out of a four-weekend trial last spring that drew 900 visitors.”
steps: The first sentence ends on new information: Sunday hours.
B begins with “the new hours,” which the reader just learned about, and ends with the new fact, the trial.
A begins with a trial the reader has never heard of, then has to circle back.
blocks.a: B: it starts with the old information and ends with the new.

items: Underline the first few words of each sentence: its starting point.
Ask whether that starting point appeared in the sentence before. If not, look for a way to begin with something that did.
Move the new, important information toward the end, where it can hand off to the next sentence.

blocks.html: Jumping to a new topic at the start of every sentence, so the paragraph feels like a list of separate facts. Check: underline the first few words of each sentence. Do they point back to something in the sentence before? If not, try flipping the sentence (sometimes with the passive voice, which exists partly for this).

blocks.html: Register is the level of formality of your language. It is part of diction, fitted to the audience: a text to a friend, an email to a teacher and a letter to the city council call for different registers.

Informal
Formal

can’t, won’t, it’s
cannot, will not, it is

blocks.html: Match the register to the audience and occasion, and keep it steady. Formal doesn’t mean fancy: clear, plain words in complete sentences are formal enough for almost any reader.

Register signals respect and seriousness. Slang in a letter to the council suggests you aren’t taking the request seriously; stiff, fancy language to a friend sounds cold. A sudden shift in register (a slang word in a formal essay) jars the reader out of the argument.

blocks.title: From stuffy to formal and clear
blocks.q: Revise: “It is to be hoped that consideration will be given by the board to the utilization of the facility on Sundays.”
steps: The sentence is stiff: passive voice, abstract nouns (consideration, utilization), and no clear doer.
Formal doesn’t require any of that. Name the doer and use plain verbs.
blocks.a: “I hope the board will consider opening the library on Sundays.”

blocks.title: Too casual for the occasion
blocks.q: An email to a principal: “Hey! So the late bus is like super packed lol, can u fix it?”
steps: Greeting, slang (super packed, lol), a texting spelling (u) and a demand.
Formal and clear: a greeting, a complete sentence about the problem, a polite request.
blocks.a: “Dear Ms. Patel, the late bus has been full most days this month. Could the school add a second one?”

blocks.html: Thinking formal writing means long words and the passive voice. That produces stiff prose that is harder to read, not more serious. Contractions are a judgment call: many teachers ask you to avoid them in academic essays, and they are fine in most other writing, including much published prose. Check: would a respected adult reader find this both clear and respectful?

blocks.html: Figures of speech are another part of diction: words used beyond their literal meaning to make a reader see or feel something.

head: Figure
What it does
Example

says one thing is another
“it is not light that is needed, but fire” (Douglass)
Simile
compares with like or as
The empty gym was as quiet as a library on Sunday.

blocks.html: Choose a figure for its effect: a fresh picture that makes an idea clearer or stronger. Keep each figure consistent, and skip the ones worn out by use.

A good figure does in a few words what a paragraph of explanation might not. When Douglass says the nation needs “fire” rather than “light,” listeners feel the difference between gentle teaching and burning rebuke at once.

blocks.title: Name it and say what it does
blocks.q: Lincoln, 1865: “… to bind up the nation’s wounds; to care for him who shall have borne the battle …” What figure is “the nation’s wounds,” and what does it do?
steps: A nation can’t literally have wounds; the phrase treats it as a body.
That is personification (some call it metaphor).
Effect: the country becomes something to heal, not to punish, which fits Lincoln’s call for “charity for all.”
blocks.a: Personification: the nation as a wounded body to be healed.

blocks.html: Mixing metaphors (“We need to nip this problem in the bud before it snowballs out of control,” where a plant becomes a snowball), or reaching for clichés that no longer make a picture (“at the end of the day,” “think outside the box”). Check: picture each figure literally. Does the picture hold together, and is it one your reader hasn’t seen a hundred times?

blocks.html: You have met Strunk’s rules in Concision and Active and Passive Voice. William Strunk Jr., an English professor at Cornell, wrote The Elements of Style in 1918 as a short handbook for his students. The 1918 text is in the public domain; the expanded “Strunk and White” edition (E. B. White, 1959 and later) is a different, newer book.

head: Rule (1918)
What it is for
rows: 10. As a rule, begin each paragraph with a topic sentence; end it in conformity with the beginning.
readers know what each paragraph is about
11. Use the active voice.
the doer and the action come first
12. Put statements in positive form.
“He usually came late,” not “He was not very often on time”
13. Omit needless words.
every word does work
15. Express co-ordinate ideas in similar form.
parallel ideas look parallel
18. Place the emphatic words of a sentence at the end.
the point rings longest
blocks.cap: Six of Strunk’s ten principles of composition.

blocks.html: Classic style rules are rules of thumb for clear writing. Know what each rule is for; then you can follow it nearly always, and break it when breaking it serves the reader better.

Strunk said so himself, in his introduction: “It is an old observation that the best writers sometimes disregard the rules of rhetoric. When they do so, however, the reader will usually find in the sentence some compensating merit, attained at the cost of the violation. Unless he is certain of doing as well, he will probably do best to follow the rules.”

blocks.title: A good reason to break a rule
blocks.q: Rule 11 says “Use the active voice.” In a paragraph about the town’s oldest bridge, a student writes: “The bridge was built in 1911 by local stonemasons.” Should she change it to active?
steps: The paragraph is about the bridge, so the bridge belongs in the subject position.
The passive keeps the focus where it belongs. That is a compensating merit.
Strunk gives the same kind of example: which voice depends on what the paragraph is about.
blocks.a: No: the passive serves the paragraph’s focus, which is a good reason to keep it.

blocks.title: Follow the rule
blocks.q: Rule 12: “Put statements in positive form.” Revise: “The plan was not without some problems that were not small.”
steps: Double negatives (not without, not small) make the reader do arithmetic.
Say what is, positively.
blocks.a: “The plan had serious problems.”

blocks.html: Treating rules of thumb as laws. Strunk wrote that the best writers sometimes break the rules, for some compensating merit. Some modern linguists, such as Geoffrey Pullum (2009), have also criticized parts of the book’s grammar advice. Check: when you break a rule, can you name what the reader gains? If not, follow the rule.

blocks.html: Every assignment, exam question and application is a small rhetorical situation with you as the writer and the prompt-setter as the audience. Rhetorical analysis taught you to read a text for its purpose; read a prompt the same way, before you plan a word.

items: The task word: what you must do. Argue (defend, challenge or qualify), analyze, explain, compare, evaluate, synthesize.
The subject: what you must write about, often narrower than the topic.
The limits: use at least three sources, refer to the passage, write a single essay, the time allowed.

blocks.name: wr-mark

sentences.text: Read the following excerpt from Lincoln’s Second Inaugural Address, given on March 4, 1865.
Write an essay that analyzes the rhetorical choices Lincoln makes to prepare his audience for reconciliation.
Support your analysis with evidence from the passage.

blocks.cap: A practice prompt in the style of an AP analysis question, with its parts marked.

blocks.html: Before you plan, find the task word, the subject and the limits. Answer the task, not just the topic.

A beautiful essay that does the wrong task earns little credit. A prompt about Lincoln’s choices asks how he persuades, not whether the war was just; an essay arguing the second question, however strong, has missed the first.

head: Task word
It asks you to
rows: argue / defend, challenge or qualify
take a position and support it; qualify means agree in part
analyze
explain how a text’s choices work for its purpose
explain
make something clear, without arguing for a side
synthesize
combine several sources in support of your own position
evaluate
judge strengths and weaknesses by criteria

blocks.title: Find the task
blocks.q: Prompt: “Many towns debate whether to plant trees along their main streets. Write an essay that argues your position on the extent to which towns should spend money on street trees.”
steps: Task word: argues your position. This is an argument essay.
Subject: how far towns should spend money on street trees, not trees in general.
“The extent to which” invites a qualified position, not only yes or no.
blocks.a: Argue a position (possibly qualified) on how much towns should spend on street trees.

blocks.html: Answering the topic instead of the task: arguing when the prompt says analyze, or summarizing when it says argue. Check: circle the task word and write it at the top of your plan; reread it before your conclusion.

blocks.html: Timed writing combines reading the prompt and building an argument under a clock. On the AP English Language exam, as given today, students write three essays (synthesis, rhetorical analysis and argument) in two hours and fifteen minutes, including a 15-minute reading period: about 40 minutes per essay.

blocks.name: wr-checklist

blocks.html: Read the prompt closely, plan for about a tenth of the time, state a clear thesis early, give each reason a paragraph with evidence and commentary, and save a few minutes to reread.

Planning feels like lost time, but it saves time: an essay with a plan doesn’t wander, and a clear thesis tells the reader (and you) what every paragraph is for. The reread catches the missing word or wrong name that would make a reader doubt you.

head: Step
Minutes

Plan: thesis and two or three reasons
Write
Reread and fix

blocks.title: Running out of time
blocks.q: Ten minutes are left and you have written two body paragraphs of a planned three. What should you do?
steps: A missing conclusion leaves the essay unfinished; a missing third reason only makes it shorter.
Write a short third paragraph (or fold its point into a sentence) and a two-sentence conclusion.
Use the last minutes to reread for errors.
blocks.a: Finish the essay: a brief last point, a short conclusion, then a quick reread.

blocks.html: Starting to write at once and drifting from the prompt, or running out of time before the conclusion. Check: before writing, can you say your thesis in one sentence and name your reasons? Glance at the clock at the end of each paragraph.

blocks.html: A college application essay is a personal essay. It draws on narrative writing and on choosing the right register: your own voice, careful but not stiff. This topic gives general guidance only; always follow the instructions and limits of the application you are filling out.
Tell one specific story and reflect on what it shows about you, in your own voice. The essay should reveal something about you that the rest of the application can’t.

The rest of an application already lists grades, activities and awards. The essay is the one place a reader meets you: how you think, what you notice, what you care about. A list repeats what they know; a story shows them someone new.

items: Narrow: one moment, one object, one conversation, rather than your whole life.
Show, then reflect: tell the story with specific details, then say what it meant and how it changed what you do or think.
Your voice: write the way you would explain it to a teacher you respect, not the way you imagine an admissions officer talks.
Answer the prompt the application gives, within its limits.
Revise and proofread: read it aloud; ask a trusted reader whether it sounds like you.

blocks.title: Résumé or story?
blocks.q: Which opening is more promising? (A) “I have been class treasurer, captain of the swim team and a volunteer at the food bank.” (B) “The first time I counted the food bank’s cans alone, I found we had 300 cans of beans and no can openers.”
steps: A lists achievements already shown elsewhere in the application.
B starts with a specific, surprising moment, and invites reflection: what did the writer notice, and what did they do next?
blocks.a: B: a specific moment the writer can reflect on.

blocks.html: Listing achievements, a résumé in paragraphs, instead of telling one story and reflecting on what it shows. Check: could someone else with the same activities have written your essay? If yes, find the moment only you could tell.
